</section>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3 </span>Spectral analysis</h3>

<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The matrix <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{h}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>h</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{h}</annotation></semantics></math> in <a href="#S3.E9" title="Equation 9 ‣ Low-rank communication. ‣ 3.2 FLARE: Fast Low-rank Attention Routing Engine ‣ 3 Method ‣ FLARE: Fast Low-rank Attention Routing Engine" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Eq. 9</span></a> represents the attention weights between <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math> tokens, where <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[W_{h}]_{ij}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>h</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[W_{h}]_{ij}</annotation></semantics></math> quantifies how much token <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="j" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>j</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">j</annotation></semantics></math> communicates to token <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math> within head <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>h</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h</annotation></semantics></math>.
Since <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{h}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>h</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{h}</annotation></semantics></math> has rank at most <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math>, the model can capture at most <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> independent global communication patterns per head.
The eigenvalues of <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>W</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W</annotation></semantics></math> indicate the relative importance or energy of each latent dimension in forming the attention matrix <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>W</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W</annotation></semantics></math>.
We apply an algorithm to obtain the eigendecomposition of <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>W</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W</annotation></semantics></math> in <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{O}(M^{3}+M^{2}N)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>M</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mrow><msup><mi>M</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}(M^{3}+M^{2}N)</annotation></semantics></math> time compared to <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{O}(N^{3})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>N</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}(N^{3})</annotation></semantics></math> for a dense communication matrix.
The algorithm is predicated on computing the eigenspectra of an <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M\times M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M\times M</annotation></semantics></math> matrix <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="JJ^{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>J</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>J</mi><mi>T</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">JJ^{T}</annotation></semantics></math>
where <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="J\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times N}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>J</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">J\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times N}</annotation></semantics></math> is chosen such that <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m18" class="ltx_Math" alttext="J^{T}J" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>J</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>J</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">J^{T}J</annotation></semantics></math> is similar to <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m19" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>W</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W</annotation></semantics></math>.
The algorithm is detailed in <a href="#A3.SS1" title="C.1 Eigenanalysis procedure ‣ Appendix C Spectral analysis ‣ FLARE: Fast Low-rank Attention Routing Engine" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section C.1</span></a>, and summarized in Algorithm 1.
<a href="#A7.F12" title="Figure 12 ‣ Number of blocks (𝐵) and latent tokens (𝑀). ‣ Appendix G Model analysis and ablations ‣ FLARE: Fast Low-rank Attention Routing Engine" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure 12</span></a> presents the <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m20" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> nonzero eigenvalues of <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m21" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{h}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>h</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{h}</annotation></semantics></math> for an FLARE model trained on the Elasticity benchmark problem with 972 points per input.
The distinct spectra of the heads indicates that each head learns distinct attention patterns.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The eigenvalue analysis detailed in <a href="#A3.SS2" title="C.2 Qualitative Analysis ‣ Appendix C Spectral analysis ‣ FLARE: Fast Low-rank Attention Routing Engine" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section C.2</span></a> shows that while FLARE provides capacity for rank-<math id="S3.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> attention, the model learns to use only a small fraction of this in early blocks indicating effective compression.
In deeper blocks, more of the latent capacity is utilized, with diverse spectral profiles across heads, validating our design choice of independent head-wise projections.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Benchmark dataset for additive manufacturing</h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We introduce a benchmark dataset of <em id="S4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">laser powder bed fusion</em> (LPBF) simulations designed to evaluate surrogate models on large, irregular 3D geometries.
LPBF is a widely used metal additive manufacturing process in which a laser fuses thin layers of powder, producing complex parts but often inducing <em id="S4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">residual stresses</em> and <em id="S4.p1.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">distortions</em> that can lead to build failures <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., </a>)</cite>.
To capture these effects, we simulate the thermo–mechanical LPBF process on thousands of geometries drawn from the Fusion 360 segmentation dataset <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lambourne et al., 2021</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Our benchmark task is <em id="S4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">predicting vertical (<math id="S4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Z" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>Z</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Z</annotation></semantics></math>) displacement field</em> for each geometry, a quantity directly associated with recoater-blade collisions and build-failure risk in LPBF.
Each sample consists of the 3D mesh coordinates as input and the final <math id="S4.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Z" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>Z</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Z</annotation></semantics></math>-displacement at all nodes as output.
The dataset spans a wide variety of part shapes, mesh resolutions, and deformation magnitudes, making it a challenging and practically meaningful testbed for large-scale surrogate modeling.
Additional details such as statistics and visualizations are provided in <a href="#A8" title="Appendix H Benchmark dataset of additive manufacturing simulations ‣ FLARE: Fast Low-rank Attention Routing Engine" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Appendix H</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Experiments</h2>

<section id="S5.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.1 </span>PDE surrogate benchmarks</h3>

<section id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Benchmark problems.</h4>

<div id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We consider a diverse set of benchmark datasets (<a href="#A4.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ D.1 Benchmark metrics ‣ Appendix D Benchmarking and Comparison ‣ FLARE: Fast Low-rank Attention Routing Engine" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table 3</span></a>) for regressing PDE solutions on point clouds spanning structured and unstructured grids with up to 50,000 points.
Note that FLARE is mesh-agnostic, and operates solely on the input point cloud.
The 2D Elasticity, Darcy, Airfoil, and Pipe benchmarks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2023b</a>)</cite> cover a wide range of physical phenomena, and the 3D DrivAerML benchmark <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ashton et al., 2024</a>)</cite> provides automotive aerodynamic simulations.
Visualizations of the Elasticity, Darcy, and Pipe benchmark problems are presented in <a href="#S3.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ Overall design. ‣ 3.2 FLARE: Fast Low-rank Attention Routing Engine ‣ 3 Method ‣ FLARE: Fast Low-rank Attention Routing Engine" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure 4</span></a>.
Additional details of the dataset are presented in <a href="#A4.SS2" title="D.2 Benchmark datasets ‣ Appendix D Benchmarking and Comparison ‣ FLARE: Fast Low-rank Attention Routing Engine" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section D.2</span></a>.
We also introduce a 3D field-prediction benchmark derived from laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) simulations, with diverse 3D-printed parts containing up to 50,000 grid points (see <a href="#A8" title="Appendix H Benchmark dataset of additive manufacturing simulations ‣ FLARE: Fast Low-rank Attention Routing Engine" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Appendix H</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.F5" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2508.12594v3/scale_dml.svg" id="S5.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/132;" width="476" height="132"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S5.F5.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 5</span>: </span><span id="S5.F5.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">
We train FLARE on the DrivAerML dataset <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ashton et al., 2024</a>)</cite> with one million points per geometry on a single Nvidia H100 80GB GPU.
We present (left) the test relative error, (middle) time per epoch (s), and
(right) peak memory utilization (GB) as a function of the number of FLARE blocks (<math id="S5.F5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>B</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B</annotation></semantics></math>) for different number of latent tokens (<math id="S5.F5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math>).
</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Baselines.</h4>

<div id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We compare FLARE with state-of-the-art PDE surrogates: generic attention models (vanilla Transformer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Vaswani et al., 2017</a>)</cite>, PerceiverIO <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jaegle et al., 2021a</a>)</cite>); attention-based PDE surrogates (Transolver <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, LNO <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang and Wang, 2024a</a>)</cite>); and the neural operator GNOT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hao et al., 2023</a>)</cite>.
We exclude graph-based models because graph connectivity is unavailable for most problems.
Transolver++ <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Luo et al., 2025</a>)</cite> is a concurrent work; we tested the official implementation with reported hyperparameters, but were unable to reproduce the reported numbers, so we do not include it in our comparisons (details in <a href="#A4.SS3" title="D.3 Benchmark models and training details ‣ Appendix D Benchmarking and Comparison ‣ FLARE: Fast Low-rank Attention Routing Engine" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section D.3</span></a>).
We follow the experimental setup of Transolver as it is the preeminent surrogate model and attempt to match its parameter count.
Note that Transolver can be instantiated in two configurations: <em id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">without convolution</em>, where point-to-point communication relies solely on physics attention,
and <em id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">with convolution</em>, where convolution layers are added to inject information from neighboring points when the input grid is structured.
We evaluate these two configurations separately to isolate the impact of convolution versus physics attention.
In our model, we choose not to employ any convolution layers and rely entirely on FLARE for token mixing. Because these PDE problems are relatively small (up to 50,000 points), we train all models in FP32. As shown in <a href="#A4.F8" title="Figure 8 ‣ FLARE. ‣ D.3 Benchmark models and training details ‣ Appendix D Benchmarking and Comparison ‣ FLARE: Fast Low-rank Attention Routing Engine" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure 8</span></a>, the vanilla Transformer is drastically slower than FLARE and Transolver on large point clouds; accordingly, we evaluate it only on problems up to <math id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim 10{,}000" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>∼</mo><mn>10,000</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim 10{,}000</annotation></semantics></math> points.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Discussion.</h4>

<div id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The results in <a href="#S3.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ Low-rank communication. ‣ 3.2 FLARE: Fast Low-rank Attention Routing Engine ‣ 3 Method ‣ FLARE: Fast Low-rank Attention Routing Engine" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table 1</span></a> clearly demonstrate that the proposed FLARE architecture achieves the lowest relative <math id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>L</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> error across all but one benchmark PDE problems, outperforming both LNO and Transolver on every dataset.
Notably, FLARE also achieves these gains with a consistently lower parameter count than Transolver or LNO, highlighting its efficiency in addition to higher accuracy.
These results underline the robustness and versatility of FLARE across diverse problem settings.
We also note that the poor performance of Transolver without convolutions indicates that the inter-point communication via Transolver’s built-in physics-attention mechanism is not enough.
With convolutions, the input projections amass information from neighboring points, which in turn helps the physics attention learn the global structure.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Although the vanilla transformer is extremely effective on small-scale PDE problems, it becomes prohibitively slow on large point clouds due to its quadratic cost as illustrated in <a href="#S1.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ FLARE: Fast Low-rank Attention Routing Engine" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure 2</span></a>.
On the contrary, PerceiverIO (with only a single encoding and decoding step) performs poorly even with <math id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M=1,024" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1,024</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M=1,024</annotation></semantics></math> latent tokens and <math id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B=8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B=8</annotation></semantics></math> latent self-attention blocks.
This validates our hypothesis that
multiple latent self-attention operations can be unnecessary and potentially suboptimal so long as the projections are sufficiently expressive.
This is because information loss during projection is not recoverable via latent self-attention alone.
Instead, performing multiple (head-wise) parallel projections and reconstructions directly between the input and latent sequences preserves expressivity while simplifying the architecture.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.T2" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S5.T2.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 2</span>: </span><span id="S5.T2.6" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">
Accuracy (%) of different transformer models on Long Range Arena benchmark tasks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tay et al., </a>)</cite>.

</section>
<section id="S5.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.2 </span>Field-prediction on million-point geometries</h3>

<div id="S5.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The benchmark problems in <a href="#S5.SS1" title="5.1 PDE surrogate benchmarks ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ FLARE: Fast Low-rank Attention Routing Engine" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section 5.1</span></a> contain a variety of PDE problems, but are relatively small compared to industrial use cases that demand PDE solutions on complex geometries with millions of grid points <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ashton et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.
So far, attention-based surrogate models have not been able to scale to million-scale regression problems due to quadratic time and memory complexity, as illustrated in <a href="#S1.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ FLARE: Fast Low-rank Attention Routing Engine" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure 2</span></a>.
The FlashAttention <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dao et al., 2022</a>)</cite> algorithm has alleviated the memory bottleneck thanks to online softmax computation; however, these methods remain impractical due to their long training times.
Furthermore, SOTA models such as Transolver and LNO are not readily expressible purely in terms of SDPA calls for their dominant <math id="S5.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{O}(NM)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}(NM)</annotation></semantics></math> projection/unprojection steps; in typical implementations these steps explicitly materialize <math id="S5.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M\times N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M\times N</annotation></semantics></math> projection weights, which prevents using PyTorch’s fused SDPA backends (e.g., FlashAttention-style kernels) for the <math id="S5.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{O}(NM)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}(NM)</annotation></semantics></math> bottleneck.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We demonstrate in <a href="#S5.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ Benchmark problems. ‣ 5.1 PDE surrogate benchmarks ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ FLARE: Fast Low-rank Attention Routing Engine" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure 5</span></a> that FLARE can scale to million-scale geometries by training on the DrivAerML dataset <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ashton et al., 2024</a>)</cite> where each mesh is subsampled to contain one million points.
These calculations are performed in mixed precision on a single Nvidia H100 80GB GPU provisioned through Google Cloud Platform.
We note the clear trend in <a href="#S5.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ Benchmark problems. ‣ 5.1 PDE surrogate benchmarks ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ FLARE: Fast Low-rank Attention Routing Engine" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure 5</span></a> (left) that the error consistently decreases as we increase the number of FLARE blocks.
To our knowledge, this is the first attention-based neural surrogate model trained on one million points on a single GPU without memory offloading or distributed computing.
Additional details are presented in <a href="#A5" title="Appendix E Field-prediction on million-point geometries ‣ FLARE: Fast Low-rank Attention Routing Engine" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Appendix E</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.3 </span>Long Range Arena benchmark problems</h3>

<div id="S5.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To demonstrate that FLARE is not limited to PDE surrogate modeling, we also evaluate it on the Long Range Arena (LRA) benchmark suite <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tay et al., </a>)</cite>, which covers a diverse set of long-context tasks ranging from logical reasoning and text classification to retrieval, image classification, and visual pathfinding.
While many top-performing LRA models rely on architectures specialized for 1D sequence structure (e.g., linear-attention kernels and state-space models such as MEGA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ma et al., 2022</a>)</cite> and Mamba <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gu and Dao, </a>)</cite>), these methods typically assume an inherent token ordering and are therefore not directly applicable to the unordered point clouds and unstructured meshes that motivate this work.
In contrast, FLARE is fully permutation-equivariant and makes no such structural assumptions.
As shown in Table <a href="#S5.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ Discussion. ‣ 5.1 PDE surrogate benchmarks ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ FLARE: Fast Low-rank Attention Routing Engine" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, FLARE achieves the highest average accuracy among the attention baselines we evaluate, outperforming general-purpose efficient-attention mechanisms (Linformer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2020</a>)</cite>, Performer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Choromanski et al., 2020</a>)</cite>, Norm Attention <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qin et al., 2022</a>)</cite>, Linear Attention) and even vanilla self-attention on average.
These results indicate that the low-rank formulation underlying FLARE provides a robust and broadly applicable inductive bias, extending beyond PDE surrogates to heterogeneous long-range tasks.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.4 </span>Model analysis and ablation studies</h3>

<div id="S5.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We conduct focused ablations in <a href="#A7" title="Appendix G Model analysis and ablations ‣ FLARE: Fast Low-rank Attention Routing Engine" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Appendix G</span></a> that causally isolate the contribution of each component and clarify trade-offs between expressivity, time, and memory complexity.
Runnable code for all experiments, benchmarks, and ablations is provided in the supplementary material.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We first examine <span id="S5.SS4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">time and memory scaling</span> as a function of sequence length.
FLARE exhibits true linear <math id="S5.SS4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{O}(NM)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}(NM)</annotation></semantics></math> scaling in both runtime and peak memory usage, even up to one million tokens.
This behavior follows directly from FLARE’s SDPA-compatible formulation, which avoids materializing attention matrices or <math id="S5.SS4.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M\times N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M\times N</annotation></semantics></math> projection weights and allocates sequence-length–dependent memory only for input activations.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS4.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Next, we study the trade-off between <span id="S5.SS4.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">model depth and latent dimensionality</span>.
Across all PDE benchmarks, including the 1M-point DrivAerML dataset, accuracy improves consistently with more encode–decode blocks, while increasing the number of latent tokens <math id="S5.SS4.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> yields diminishing returns except on inherently high-rank tasks.
This demonstrates that repeated low-rank mixing through depth is a more effective driver of global communication than increasing the rank of a single attention operator.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS4.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS4.p4.1" class="ltx_p">We then evaluate <span id="S5.SS4.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">head-wise parallel low-rank pathways</span>.
Varying the number of attention heads while keeping total width fixed shows that FLARE performs best with many small heads rather than a few large ones, indicating that aggregating multiple independent low-rank operators approximates richer attention patterns than concentrating capacity into fewer projections.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS4.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS4.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Next, we compare <span id="S5.SS4.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">latent-space self-attention versus encode–decode blocks</span> and find that latent self-attention consistently worsens accuracy and increases computation, whereas adding encode–decode blocks improves performance; the best results occur when latent self-attention is entirely removed.
Then, we study <span id="S5.SS4.p5.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">shared versus independent latent tokens</span> and observe that sharing latents across heads collapses the induced spectra and degrades accuracy, while independent latent slices yield diverse eigenvalue decay profiles and lower error.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS4.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS4.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Together, these ablations validate FLARE’s architectural choices: explicit low-rank operator factorization, repeated encode-decode mixing, and head-wise latent independence. Its gains, therefore, do not stem from increased parameter count or implementation-level optimizations.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">FLARE is a token mixing layer that bypasses the quadratic cost of self-attention by leveraging low-rankness.
Mechanically, FLARE routes attention through a fixed-size latent sequence via cross-attention projection and unprojection.
FLARE achieves SOTA accuracy on a set of diverse PDE benchmarks, and easily scales to PDE problems with million-scale geometries.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p2.1" class="ltx_p">As transformers are the backbone of modern deep learning, we postulate that an efficient attention mechanism has several applications.
We also identify potential areas for improvement:
FLARE’s reliance on deep residual MLPs can introduce sequential bottlenecks and increase latency, suggesting that further speedups are possible by addressing this issue.
Additional enhancements include
(1) incrementally increasing the number of latent tokens during training;
(2) conditioning the latent queries/tokens on the input to relax the fixed-<math id="S6.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Q" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>Q</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q</annotation></semantics></math> constraint;
(3) conditioning latent tokens on time for diffusion modeling;
and
(4) designing decoder-only variants for autoregressive modeling.</p>
</div>
</section>

The authors appreciate the support of Camfer, Inc. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Camfer, 2025</a>)</cite> and Professor Amir Barati Farimani in providing computing resources.
Part of this research was conducted on the Bridges-2 Supercomputer at the Pittsburgh Supercomputing Center, and parts were conducted using ORCHARD, a high-performance cloud computing cluster made available by Carnegie Mellon University.
The authors thank Jay Pathak of Ansys, Inc. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ansys, 2025</a>)</cite> for insightful discussions, undergraduate researcher Andrew Porco for his assistance with data processing.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="Sx2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section">Impact Statement</h2>

<div id="Sx2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Self-attention underpins many modern AI systems, but its quadratic computational and memory cost makes both training and inference expensive and difficult to scale.
By making attention-based models practical on very large inputs within single-GPU workflows, FLARE lowers the barrier to deploying powerful sequence models across a wide range of applications.</p>
</div>
</section>

<td id="A1.F6.3.1.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_tt"><span id="A1.F6.3.1.5.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">FLARE</span></td></tr>

<ul id="A1.I1" class="ltx_itemize ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel">
<li id="A1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">*Evaluating cost of processing </span><math id="A1.I1.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N\gg M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathsize="0.800em">N</mi><mo mathsize="0.800em">≫</mo><mi mathsize="0.800em">M</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N\gg M</annotation></semantics></math><span id="A1.I1.i1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;"> tokens ignoring feedforward layers (FFN are </span><math id="A1.I1.i1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{O}(N)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic" mathsize="0.800em">𝒪</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="0.800em" minsize="0.800em">(</mo><mi mathsize="0.800em">N</mi><mo maxsize="0.800em" minsize="0.800em">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}(N)</annotation></semantics></math><span id="A1.I1.i1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">).</span></p>
</div></li>
<li id="A1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><sup id="A1.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_sup"><span id="A1.I1.i2.p1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">†</span></sup><span id="A1.I1.i2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">Physics Attention in Transolver uses the same projection weights for all heads,
whereas PerceiverIO and FLARE use cross-attention projection where each head learns
a distinct slice of the latent tokens.</span></p>
</div></li>
</ul></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering" style="font-size:80%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A1.F6.21" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:113%;">Figure 6</span>: </span><span id="A1.F6.22" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:113%;">
Comparison of
(a) PerceiverIO <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jaegle et al., 2021a</a>)</cite>,
(b) Transolver <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al., 2024</a>)</cite>,
(c) LNO <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang and Wang, 2024b</a>)</cite>, and
(d) FLARE (ours).
Each model contains <math id="A1.F6.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>B</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B</annotation></semantics></math> blocks and <math id="A1.F6.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> latents.
The criteria in the table are described in detail in <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A Extended related work ‣ FLARE: Fast Low-rank Attention Routing Engine" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Appendix A</span></a>.
</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><a href="#A1.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ Appendix A Extended related work ‣ FLARE: Fast Low-rank Attention Routing Engine" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure 6</span></a>provides a structural and computational comparison between PerceiverIO <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jaegle et al. (2021a)</a></cite>, Transolver <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al. (2024)</a></cite>, Latent Neural Operator (LNO) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang and Wang (2024a)</a></cite>, and FLARE.
All four architectures introduce a latent bottleneck to reduce the quadratic cost of self-attention, but they differ fundamentally in how latent tokens are used, how information is mixed across tokens, and how the resulting attention operator is realized and implemented.</p>
</div>
<section id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Perceiver and PerceiverIO.</h4>

<div id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Perceiver and PerceiverIO <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jaegle et al., 2021b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jaegle et al., 2021a</a>)</cite> introduce a general latent-attention framework in which a fixed-size latent array of length <math id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> attends to an input sequence of length <math id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math> via cross-attention.
This step maps the input into latent space, after which multiple layers of latent self-attention are applied.
Optionally, PerceiverIO performs additional cross-attention from the latent array back to the input or output tokens.
This design reduces the cost of attention on the input sequence and enables flexible input and output modalities.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">However, Perceiver-style models use latent tokens as a <em id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">computational workspace</em>: information is repeatedly transformed within the latent space through self-attention.
As a result, the effective input-input communication pattern is a deep composition of latent transformations rather than a single, explicit attention operator.
While expressive, this structure makes it difficult to characterize the induced token-to-token interactions or to interpret the model as implementing a specific low-rank attention operator on the input sequence.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Transolver and Latent Neural Operator.</h4>

<div id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Transolver <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al., 2024</a>)</cite> and Latent Neural Operator (LNO) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang and Wang, 2024a</a>)</cite> adapt latent-attention ideas specifically for PDE surrogate modeling on point clouds and meshes.
Both architectures project variable-length inputs into a fixed-length latent representation and use latent self-attention to aggregate global information.
A key difference from PerceiverIO is that Transolver performs projection and unprojection in <em id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">every</em> transformer block, allowing global context to accumulate progressively with depth.
LNO, by contrast, performs a single projection-unprojection step followed by latent self-attention.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In practice, both Transolver and LNO rely on feature-projection mechanisms that explicitly construct or manipulate <math id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M\times N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M\times N</annotation></semantics></math> projection weights, typically via feature expansion followed by attention or linear layers.
These projection layers introduce additional memory and compute overhead that becomes significant for large <math id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math>.
Moreover, both models rely on latent-space self-attention as the primary mechanism for global mixing, which introduces an <math id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{O}(M^{2})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>M</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}(M^{2})</annotation></semantics></math> cost per block.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We note that Transolver can be instantiated with or without convolutional layers.
Without convolution, point-to-point communication relies solely on physics attention; with convolution, local neighborhood aggregation is explicitly injected before attention.
We evaluate both configurations separately to disentangle the effects of convolutional inductive bias and latent attention.
Our results in <a href="#S3.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ Low-rank communication. ‣ 3.2 FLARE: Fast Low-rank Attention Routing Engine ‣ 3 Method ‣ FLARE: Fast Low-rank Attention Routing Engine" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table 1</span></a> show that Transolver without convolution performs poorly, indicating that its physics-attention mechanism alone is insufficient for effective global communication.
When convolutions are included, local aggregation significantly improves performance, suggesting that much of the gain arises from convolutional preprocessing rather than latent attention itself.
In contrast, FLARE does not rely on any convolutional layers and achieves strong performance using attention-based token mixing alone.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">FLARE: latent routing as a low-rank operator.</h4>

<div id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">FLARE differs from prior latent-attention architectures in how latent tokens are used.
Rather than serving as a computational workspace, latent tokens in FLARE act purely as a <em id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">routing mechanism</em>.
Each block consists of exactly two cross-attention operations (encode and decode) that together induce an explicit rank-<math id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\leq M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≤</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\leq M</annotation></semantics></math> linear operator on the input tokens.
FLARE eliminates latent-space self-attention entirely, ensuring that all token mixing occurs in the input space through a single encode-decode factorization.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">A further distinction is FLARE’s use of <em id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">head-wise independent latent slices</em>.
Each attention head projects into its own latent subspace, forming multiple parallel low-rank projection-reconstruction pathways.
This contrasts with Transolver, which shares projection weights across heads, and LNO, which uses a single global projection.
As shown in our spectral analysis and ablations, head-wise independence enables different heads to specialize in complementary low-rank routing patterns rather than collapsing into a shared subspace.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Summary of architectural trade-offs.</h4>

<div id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As summarized in <a href="#A1.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ Appendix A Extended related work ‣ FLARE: Fast Low-rank Attention Routing Engine" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure 6</span></a>, FLARE combines several desirable properties of prior approaches while avoiding their key limitations.
Like Transolver, it performs encode-decode operations in every block, enabling progressive global mixing.
Like PerceiverIO, it relies on cross-attention and is fully compatible with fused SDPA kernels.
Unlike all three prior methods, FLARE eliminates latent self-attention and uses head-wise independent latent routing, yielding a simple, interpretable, and strictly linear-time attention operator.
These differences explain both FLARE’s scalability to extreme sequence lengths and its strong empirical performance.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Below we briefly clarify the criteria used in <a href="#A1.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ Appendix A Extended related work ‣ FLARE: Fast Low-rank Attention Routing Engine" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure 6</span></a>.
Asymptotic evaluation cost refers to the dominant attention-related complexity for processing <math id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N\gg M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>≫</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N\gg M</annotation></semantics></math> tokens with <math id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>B</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B</annotation></semantics></math> blocks, ignoring feed-forward layers which are linear in <math id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math>.
The remaining criteria describe architectural structure rather than cost.
Sequential encode-decode blocks indicate whether global context is progressively refined across depth (as in Transolver and FLARE).
Head-wise parallel encode-decode denotes whether each attention head learns an independent latent projection, which is true for PerceiverIO and FLARE but not for Transolver or LNO.
Encoder/decoder coupling refers to whether encoding and decoding projections are tied, and latent space attention indicates the presence of explicit self-attention over latent tokens.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Finally, fused-attention compatibility captures whether all attention operations can be expressed using standard scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) primitives.
PerceiverIO and FLARE satisfy this property, enabling efficient fused implementations, whereas Transolver and LNO rely on additional projection operations that limit hardware efficiency at large <math id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math>.
Note that Transolver can employ fused SDPA kernels for latent-space self-attention (<math id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{O}(M^{2})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>M</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}(M^{2})</annotation></semantics></math>). However, encoding and decoding (<math id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{O}(NM)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}(NM)</annotation></semantics></math>) operations, which form the bottleneck in these computations, are implemented with linear projections and cannot employ SDPA kernels.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A2" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix B </span>Architecture details</h2>

<section id="A2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.1 </span>Input/ output projection</h3>

<section id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">ResMLP.</h4>

<div id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We implement a residual MLP block to serve as a flexible non-linear function approximator.
Given input/output dimensions <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C_{\text{i}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>C</mi><mtext>i</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C_{\text{i}}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C_{\text{o}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>C</mi><mtext>o</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C_{\text{o}}</annotation></semantics></math>, the layer first applies a linear transformation to a hidden space of size <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C_{\text{h}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>C</mi><mtext>h</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C_{\text{h}}</annotation></semantics></math>, followed by <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>L</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L</annotation></semantics></math> residual layers, each consisting of a linear layer with GELU activation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hendrycks and Gimpel, 2016</a>)</cite>.
These are the only instances of pointwise nonlinear activations in the model.
An optional input residual connection is applied after the first layer when <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C_{\text{i}}=C_{\text{h}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mtext>i</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mtext>h</mtext></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C_{\text{i}}=C_{\text{h}}</annotation></semantics></math>, and an optional output residual connection is applied at the end when
<math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C_{\text{h}}=C_{\text{o}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mtext>h</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mtext>o</mtext></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C_{\text{h}}=C_{\text{o}}</annotation></semantics></math>.
The final output is projected to dimension <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C_{\text{o}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>C</mi><mtext>o</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C_{\text{o}}</annotation></semantics></math> via a linear layer.
This design allows control over depth and expressivity while preserving stability through residual connections.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Input projection.</h4>

<div id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The input projection consists of a ResMLP with <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L=2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L=2</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> is the input feature dimension, and <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C_{\text{h}}=C_{\text{o}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mtext>h</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mtext>o</mtext></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C_{\text{h}}=C_{\text{o}}</annotation></semantics></math> are set to <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>C</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C</annotation></semantics></math>, the feature dimension of the model.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Output projection.</h4>

<div id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The output projection consists of a Layer Norm <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ba et al., 2016</a>)</cite> followed by a ResMLP with <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C_{\text{i}}=C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mtext>i</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C_{\text{i}}=C</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L=2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L=2</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C_{\text{o}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>C</mi><mtext>o</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C_{\text{o}}</annotation></semantics></math> is the output label dimension.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.2 </span>FLARE block</h3>

<div id="A2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The FLARE block illustrated in <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ FLARE: Fast Low-rank Attention Routing Engine" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure 1</span></a>, and detailed in <a href="#S3" title="3 Method ‣ FLARE: Fast Low-rank Attention Routing Engine" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section 3</span></a>, consists of the pointwise ResMLP layer, and the FLARE token mixer.
For the ResMLP, we set <math id="A2.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C_{\text{i}}=C_{\text{h}}=C_{\text{o}}=C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mtext>i</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mtext>h</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mtext>o</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C_{\text{i}}=C_{\text{h}}=C_{\text{o}}=C</annotation></semantics></math>, set the number of layers to <math id="A2.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>3</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3</annotation></semantics></math>, and allow residuals to flow through the entire block.</p>
</div>
<section id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">FLARE.</h4>

<div id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">FLARE consists of two ResMLPs for key/value projections, the token operation described in <a href="#S3.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 3.2 FLARE: Fast Low-rank Attention Routing Engine ‣ 3 Method ‣ FLARE: Fast Low-rank Attention Routing Engine" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure 3</span></a>, and an output projection.
For the key/value projections, we set <math id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C_{\text{i}}=C_{\text{h}}=C_{\text{o}}=C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mtext>i</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mtext>h</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mtext>o</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C_{\text{i}}=C_{\text{h}}=C_{\text{o}}=C</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L=3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L=3</annotation></semantics></math>, and allow residuals to flow through the entire block.
<a href="#A3.F7" title="Figure 7 ‣ Appendix C Spectral analysis ‣ FLARE: Fast Low-rank Attention Routing Engine" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure 7</span></a> presents a mathematically equivalent PyTorch implementation for multi-head token-mixing operation without the fused SDPA kernels.
The primary memory bottleneck in this implementation is materializing the <math id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M\times N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M\times N</annotation></semantics></math> encoding weights and the <math id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N\times M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N\times M</annotation></semantics></math> decoding weights.
Its storage requirement is, thus, <math id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{O}(MN)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}(MN)</annotation></semantics></math>.
Finally, the output projection is set to a single linear layer.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A3" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix C </span>Spectral analysis</h2>

<figure id="A3.F7" class="ltx_figure">
<div id="A3.F7.3" class="ltx_listing ltx_lst_language_Python ltx_lstlisting ltx_align_center ltx_listing"><div class="ltx_listing_data"><a href="data:text/plain;base64," download="">⬇</a></div>
<div id="lstnumberx8" class="ltx_listingline"><span id="lstnumberx8.1" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_keyword ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#FF00FF;">import</span><span id="lstnumberx8.2" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:80%;"> </span><span id="lstnumberx8.3" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:80%;">torch</span><span id="lstnumberx8.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:80%;">.</span><span id="lstnumberx8.5" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:80%;">nn</span><span id="lstnumberx8.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:80%;">.</span><span id="lstnumberx8.7" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:80%;">functional</span><span id="lstnumberx8.8" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:80%;"> </span><span id="lstnumberx8.9" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:80%;">as</span><span id="lstnumberx8.10" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:80%;"> </span><span id="lstnumberx8.11" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:80%;">F</span>
</div>
<div id="lstnumberx9" class="ltx_listingline"><span id="lstnumberx9.1" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_keyword ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#FF00FF;">def</span><span id="lstnumberx9.2" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:80%;"> </span><span id="lstnumberx9.3" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:80%;">flare_multihead_mixer_inefficient</span><span id="lstnumberx9.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:80%;">(</span><span id="lstnumberx9.5" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:80%;">Q</span><span id="lstnumberx9.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:80%;">,</span><span id="lstnumberx9.7" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:80%;"> </span><span id="lstnumberx9.8" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:80%;">K</span><span id="lstnumberx9.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:80%;">,</span><span id="lstnumberx9.10" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:80%;"> </span><span id="lstnumberx9.11" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:80%;">V</span><span id="lstnumberx9.12" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:80%;">):</span>
</div>
<div id="lstnumberx10" class="ltx_listingline">
</div>

<section id="A3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">C.1 </span>Eigenanalysis procedure</h3>

<div id="A3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We exploit the low-rank structure of the global communication matrix
<math id="A3.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W=W_{\text{decode}}\cdot W_{\text{encode}}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>W</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mtext>decode</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msub><mi>W</mi><mtext>encode</mtext></msub></mrow><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W=W_{\text{decode}}\cdot W_{\text{encode}}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N}</annotation></semantics></math>
to obtain its eigendecomposition in <math id="A3.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{O}(M^{3}+M^{2}N)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>M</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mrow><msup><mi>M</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}(M^{3}+M^{2}N)</annotation></semantics></math> time, compared to the <math id="A3.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{O}(N^{3})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>N</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}(N^{3})</annotation></semantics></math> cost for a dense communication matrix.
We find the eigendecomposition of the FLARE attention matrix without actually forming the <math id="A3.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N\times N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N\times N</annotation></semantics></math> matrix.
We first note that <math id="A3.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{\text{encode}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>W</mi><mtext>encode</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{\text{encode}}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A3.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{\text{decode}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>W</mi><mtext>decode</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{\text{decode}}</annotation></semantics></math> can be written in terms of the exponentiated score matrix
<math id="A3.SS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A=\exp(Q \cdot K^T)\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times N}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>exp</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>Q</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msup><mi>K</mi><mi>T</mi></msup></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A=\exp(Q \cdot K^T)\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times N}</annotation></semantics></math> as</p>
<table id="A3.E11" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_table">
<tbody>
<tr id="A3.E11X" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A3.E11X.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle W_{\text{encode}}=\Lambda_{M}\cdot A,\text{ and }W_{\text{decode}}=\Lambda_{N}\cdot A^{T}," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>W</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>encode</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Λ</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>M</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>,</mo><mtext> and </mtext><mi>W</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>decode</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Λ</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>N</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mi>A</mi><msup><mrow></mrow><mi>T</mi></msup><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle W_{\text{encode}}=\Lambda_{M}\cdot A,\text{ and }W_{\text{decode}}=\Lambda_{N}\cdot A^{T},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equationgroup ltx_align_right">(11)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A3.SS1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where
<math id="A3.SS1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Lambda^{M}\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times M}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">Λ</mi><mi>M</mi></msup><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Lambda^{M}\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times M}</annotation></semantics></math>,
and
<math id="A3.SS1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Lambda^{N}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">Λ</mi><mi>N</mi></msup><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Lambda^{N}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N}</annotation></semantics></math>
are diagonal matrices whose entries are</p>
<table id="A3.E12" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_table">
<tbody>
<tr id="A3.E12X" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A3.E12X.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle[\Lambda_{M}]_{m}=\frac{1}{\sum_{n=1}^{N}[A]_{m,n}},\text{ and }[\Lambda_{N}]_{n}=\frac{1}{\sum_{m=1}^{M}[A]_{m,n}}." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Λ</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>M</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">]</mo><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>m</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><msubsup><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></msubsup><msub><mrow><mo lspace="0em" stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mo>,</mo><mtext> and </mtext><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Λ</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>N</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">]</mo><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><msubsup><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>M</mi></msubsup><msub><mrow><mo lspace="0em" stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle[\Lambda_{M}]_{m}=\frac{1}{\sum_{n=1}^{N}[A]_{m,n}},\text{ and }[\Lambda_{N}]_{n}=\frac{1}{\sum_{m=1}^{M}[A]_{m,n}}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equationgroup ltx_align_right">(12)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A3.SS1.p1.3" class="ltx_p">Thus we have</p>
<table id="A3.E13" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_table">
<tbody>
<tr id="A3.E13X" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A3.E13X.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle W=\Lambda_{N}A^{T}\Lambda_{M}A" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>W</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Λ</mi><mi>N</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>A</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Λ</mi><mi>M</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>A</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle W=\Lambda_{N}A^{T}\Lambda_{M}A</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equationgroup ltx_align_right">(13)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A3.SS1.p1.4" class="ltx_p">as the low-rank attention matrix.
We observe that <math id="A3.SS1.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>W</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W</annotation></semantics></math> is similar to <math id="A3.SS1.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="J^{T}J\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>J</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>J</mi></mrow><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">J^{T}J\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N}</annotation></semantics></math>
where
<math id="A3.SS1.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="J=\Lambda_{M}^{1/2}A\Lambda_{N}^{1/2}\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times N}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>J</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">Λ</mi><mi>M</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>A</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">Λ</mi><mi>N</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup></mrow><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">J=\Lambda_{M}^{1/2}A\Lambda_{N}^{1/2}\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times N}</annotation></semantics></math>.
This is because</p>

accentunder="true"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">Λ</mi><mi>M</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" <td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="2" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equationgroup ltx_align_right">(14)</span></td></tr>
