<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A3.SS1.p1.5" class="ltx_p">Thus <math id="A3.SS1.p1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="J^{T}J" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>J</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>J</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">J^{T}J</annotation></semantics></math> is symmetric, positive semi-definite, with rank at most <math id="A3.SS1.p1.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math>.
Now suppose a singular value decomposition of <math id="A3.SS1.p1.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="J" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>J</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">J</annotation></semantics></math> as
<math id="A3.SS1.p1.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="J=U\Sigma V^{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>J</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>U</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>V</mi><mi>T</mi></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">J=U\Sigma V^{T}</annotation></semantics></math> where <math id="A3.SS1.p1.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times M}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>U</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times M}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A3.SS1.p1.m18" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times M}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>V</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times M}</annotation></semantics></math> are the matrices whose columns are the left and right singular vectors of <math id="A3.SS1.p1.m19" class="ltx_Math" alttext="J" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>J</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">J</annotation></semantics></math> respectively, and <math id="A3.SS1.p1.m20" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Sigma\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times M}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Sigma\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times M}</annotation></semantics></math> is the diagonal matrix of singular values.
Then, we obtain</p>
<table id="A3.E15" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_table">
<tbody>
<tr id="A3.E15X" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A3.E15X.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle J^{T}J=V\Sigma\underbrace{U^{T}U}_{I_{M}}\Sigma V^{T}=V\Sigma^{2}V^{T}," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>J</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>J</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>V</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><munder><munder accentunder="true"><mrow><msup><mi>U</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>U</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="true">⏟</mo></munder><msub><mi>I</mi><mi>M</mi></msub></munder><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>V</mi><mi>T</mi></msup></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>V</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>V</mi><mi>T</mi></msup></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle J^{T}J=V\Sigma\underbrace{U^{T}U}_{I_{M}}\Sigma V^{T}=V\Sigma^{2}V^{T},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equationgroup ltx_align_right">(15)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A3.SS1.p1.6" class="ltx_p">and</p>
<table id="A3.E16" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_table">
<tbody>
<tr id="A3.E16X" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A3.E16X.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle W=\Lambda_{N}^{1/2}V\Sigma^{2}V^{T}\Lambda_{N}^{-1/2}." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>W</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Λ</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>N</mi></msub><msup><mrow></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mi>V</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><msup><mrow></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mi>V</mi><msup><mrow></mrow><mi>T</mi></msup><mi mathvariant="normal">Λ</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>N</mi></msub><msup><mrow></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle W=\Lambda_{N}^{1/2}V\Sigma^{2}V^{T}\Lambda_{N}^{-1/2}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equationgroup ltx_align_right">(16)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A3.SS1.p1.7" class="ltx_p">Post-multiplying both sides by <math id="A3.SS1.p1.m21" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Lambda_{N}^{1/2}V" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">Λ</mi><mi>N</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>V</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Lambda_{N}^{1/2}V</annotation></semantics></math>, we have</p>
<table id="A3.E17" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_table">
<tbody>
<tr id="A3.E17X" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A3.E17X.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle W(\Lambda_{N}^{1/2}V)=(\Lambda_{N}^{1/2}V)\Sigma^{2}." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>W</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">Λ</mi><mi>N</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>V</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">Λ</mi><mi>N</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>V</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle W(\Lambda_{N}^{1/2}V)=(\Lambda_{N}^{1/2}V)\Sigma^{2}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equationgroup ltx_align_right">(17)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A3.SS1.p1.8" class="ltx_p">Therefore, the <math id="A3.SS1.p1.m22" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> nonzero eigenvalues of <math id="A3.SS1.p1.m23" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>W</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W</annotation></semantics></math> are the squares of the singular values of <math id="A3.SS1.p1.m24" class="ltx_Math" alttext="J" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>J</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">J</annotation></semantics></math>,
and the corresponding eigenvectors are the columns of <math id="A3.SS1.p1.m25" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Lambda_{N}^{1/2}V" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">Λ</mi><mi>N</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>V</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Lambda_{N}^{1/2}V</annotation></semantics></math>.
Obtaining the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of <math id="A3.SS1.p1.m26" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>W</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W</annotation></semantics></math> this way requires the singular value decomposition of <math id="A3.SS1.p1.m27" class="ltx_Math" alttext="J\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times N}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>J</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">J\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times N}</annotation></semantics></math>.
We can do better by relating <math id="A3.SS1.p1.m28" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>V</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A3.SS1.p1.m29" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Sigma</annotation></semantics></math> to the eigen decomposition of <math id="A3.SS1.p1.m30" class="ltx_Math" alttext="JJ^{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>J</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>J</mi><mi>T</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">JJ^{T}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Consider the matrix <math id="A3.SS1.p1.m31" class="ltx_Math" alttext="JJ^{T}\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times M}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>J</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>J</mi><mi>T</mi></msup></mrow><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">JJ^{T}\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times M}</annotation></semantics></math> with singular value decomposition, we have</p>
<table id="A3.E18" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_table">
<tbody>
<tr id="A3.E18X" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A3.E18X.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle JJ^{T}=U\Sigma\underbrace{V^{T}V}_{I_{M}}\Sigma U^{T}=U\Sigma^{2}U^{T}." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>J</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>J</mi><mi>T</mi></msup></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>U</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><munder><munder accentunder="true"><mrow><msup><mi>V</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>V</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="true">⏟</mo></munder><msub><mi>I</mi><mi>M</mi></msub></munder><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>U</mi><mi>T</mi></msup></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>U</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>U</mi><mi>T</mi></msup></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle JJ^{T}=U\Sigma\underbrace{V^{T}V}_{I_{M}}\Sigma U^{T}=U\Sigma^{2}U^{T}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equationgroup ltx_align_right">(18)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A3.SS1.p1.9" class="ltx_p">We note that the nonzero eigenvalues of <math id="A3.SS1.p1.m32" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>W</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W</annotation></semantics></math> are the same as the singular values of <math id="A3.SS1.p1.m33" class="ltx_Math" alttext="JJ^{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>J</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>J</mi><mi>T</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">JJ^{T}</annotation></semantics></math>.
To obtain the eigenvectors of <math id="A3.SS1.p1.m34" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>W</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W</annotation></semantics></math>, we need an expression for <math id="A3.SS1.p1.m35" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>V</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V</annotation></semantics></math> in terms of <math id="A3.SS1.p1.m36" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>U</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A3.SS1.p1.m37" class="ltx_Math" alttext="J" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>J</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">J</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="A3.SS1.p1.m38" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Sigma</annotation></semantics></math>.
We do so by noting that</p>
<table id="A3.E19" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_table">
<tbody>
<tr id="A3.E19X" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A3.E19X.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle J^{T}U=(V\Sigma U^{T})U=V\Sigma\implies V=J^{T}U\Sigma^{-1}." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>J</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>U</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>V</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>U</mi><mi>T</mi></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>U</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>V</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">⟹</mo><mi>V</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><msup><mi>J</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>U</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle J^{T}U=(V\Sigma U^{T})U=V\Sigma\implies V=J^{T}U\Sigma^{-1}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equationgroup ltx_align_right">(19)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A3.SS1.p1.10" class="ltx_p">Therefore, the eigenvectors of <math id="A3.SS1.p1.m39" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>W</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W</annotation></semantics></math> are</p>

<tbody>
<tr id="A3.E20X" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">

<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A3.E20X.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\Lambda_{N}^{1/2}V=\Lambda_{N}^{1/2}J^{T}U\Sigma^{-1}." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">Λ</mi><mi>N</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>V</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">Λ</mi><mi>N</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>J</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>U</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\Lambda_{N}^{1/2}V=\Lambda_{N}^{1/2}J^{T}U\Sigma^{-1}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>

<div id="A3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To find the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of <math id="A3.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>W</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W</annotation></semantics></math>, one only needs to compute the eigen-decomposition of the <math id="A3.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M\times M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M\times M</annotation></semantics></math> matrix <math id="A3.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="J^{T}J" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>J</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>J</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">J^{T}J</annotation></semantics></math>.
The overall algorithm, summarized in Algorithm 1, takes
<math id="A3.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{O}(M^{3}+NM^{2})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>M</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>M</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}(M^{3}+NM^{2})</annotation></semantics></math> time where the <math id="A3.SS1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{O}(M^{3})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>M</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}(M^{3})</annotation></semantics></math> is for computing the SVD of <math id="A3.SS1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="JJ^{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>J</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>J</mi><mi>T</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">JJ^{T}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">C.2 </span>Qualitative Analysis</h3>

<div id="A3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The matrix <math id="A3.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="JJ^{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>J</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>J</mi><mi>T</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">JJ^{T}</annotation></semantics></math>, being <math id="A3.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M\times M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M\times M</annotation></semantics></math>, captures the structure of this latent space and provides insights into how these <math id="A3.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> dimensions contribute to the attention mechanism.
Large eigenvalues correspond to dominant latent dimensions that contribute significantly to attention patterns.
If some eigenvalues are small or zero, those latent dimensions contribute little, suggesting redundancy in the latent space.
The number of nonzero eigenvalues gives the effective rank of <math id="A3.SS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>W</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W</annotation></semantics></math>, which reflects how many independent patterns the attention mechanism captures.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><a href="#A7.F12" title="Figure 12 ‣ Number of blocks (𝐵) and latent tokens (𝑀). ‣ Appendix G Model analysis and ablations ‣ FLARE: Fast Low-rank Attention Routing Engine" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure 12</span></a>(middle) presents the <math id="A3.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M=64" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>64</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M=64</annotation></semantics></math> nonzero eigenvalue spectra of an FLARE model trained on the elasticity dataset with <math id="A3.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M=64" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>64</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M=64</annotation></semantics></math> latents.
Some observations are as follows.
In all blocks, especially block 1, the eigenvalues drop sharply within the first <math id="A3.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10-20" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>10</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>20</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10-20</annotation></semantics></math> indices.
This indicates that even though the communication matrices <math id="A3.SS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{h}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>h</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{h}</annotation></semantics></math> could have rank up to <math id="A3.SS2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M=64" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>64</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M=64</annotation></semantics></math>, most of the energy (information) is captured by a much smaller subset of modes.
This result validates the hypothesis that the global communication pattern is inherently low-rank.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We also observe that the eigenvalue curves in block 5 and block 8 decay more slowly, retaining more moderate-magnitude eigenvalues beyond index 20–30.
This indicates that as depth increases, the attention mechanism seems to leverage more of the latent space — i.e., the effective rank increases.
This shows that deeper layers learn richer global dependencies, and the model may be using more of the projection capacity in later blocks.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Finally, we note that the curves for different heads (colors) have distinct decay patterns, especially in later blocks.
This reinforces the claim that separate projection matrices per head enables specialized routing.
This supports the idea that FLARE benefits from head-wise diversity, rather than using shared projections like in Transolver <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A4" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix D </span>Benchmarking and Comparison</h2>

<section id="A4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">D.1 </span>Benchmark metrics</h3>

<div id="A4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The primary evaluation metric for all benchmarks is the relative <math id="A4.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> error, which quantifies the normalized discrepancy between the predicted solution <math id="A4.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{u}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>u</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{u}</annotation></semantics></math> and the ground truth solution <math id="A4.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>u</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u</annotation></semantics></math> over all points in the domain. For a given test sample, the relative <math id="A4.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>L</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> error is defined as:</p>
<table id="A4.E21" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A4.E21.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{Relative }L_{2}=\frac{\|\hat{u}-u\|_{2}}{\|u\|_{2}}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mtext>Relative </mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>L</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>u</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>−</mo><mi>u</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{Relative }L_{2}=\frac{\|\hat{u}-u\|_{2}}{\|u\|_{2}}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(21)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A4.SS1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="A4.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\|\cdot\|_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo rspace="0em">∥</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo lspace="0em">∥</mo><msub><mrow></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\|\cdot\|_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the standard Euclidean norm.
For datasets where each sample consists of <math id="A4.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math> points (or grid locations), this expands to:</p>
<table id="A4.E22" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A4.E22.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{Relative }L_{2}=\frac{\left(\sum_{i=1}^{N}(\hat{u}_{i}-u_{i})^{2}\right)^{1/2}}{\left(\sum_{i=1}^{N}u_{i}^{2}\right)^{1/2}}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mtext>Relative </mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>L</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></msubsup><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>u</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msubsup><mo lspace="0em">∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></msubsup><msubsup><mi>u</mi><mi>i</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mfrac></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{Relative }L_{2}=\frac{\left(\sum_{i=1}^{N}(\hat{u}_{i}-u_{i})^{2}\right)^{1/2}}{\left(\sum_{i=1}^{N}u_{i}^{2}\right)^{1/2}}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(22)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="A4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The reported metric is averaged over all test samples.</p>
</div>

<section id="A4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">D.2 </span>Benchmark datasets</h3>

<div id="A4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate all models on five benchmark datasets and our proposed AM dataset, each designed to assess generalization, scalability, and robustness to domain irregularity in PDE surrogate modeling. A summary is provided in <a href="#A4.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ D.1 Benchmark metrics ‣ Appendix D Benchmarking and Comparison ‣ FLARE: Fast Low-rank Attention Routing Engine" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table 3</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<section id="A4.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Elasticity.</h4>

<div id="A4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This benchmark estimates the inner stress distribution of elastic materials based on their structure. Each sample consists of a tensor of shape <math id="A4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="972\times 2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>972</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">972\times 2</annotation></semantics></math> representing the 2D coordinates of discretized points, and the output is the stress at each point (<math id="A4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="972\times 1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>972</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">972\times 1</annotation></semantics></math>). The dataset contains 1,000 training and 200 test samples with different material structures <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2023b</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A4.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Darcy.</h4>

<div id="A4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This benchmark models fluid flow through a porous medium.
The porous structure is discretized on a <math id="A4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="421\times 421" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>421</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>421</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">421\times 421</annotation></semantics></math> regular grid, downsampled to <math id="A4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="85\times 85" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>85</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>85</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">85\times 85</annotation></semantics></math> for main experiments.
The output is the fluid pressure at each grid point.
There are 1,000 training and 200 test samples with varying medium structures <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2021</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A4.SS2.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Airfoil.</h4>

<div id="A4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This task estimates the Mach number distribution around airfoil shapes. The input geometry is discretized into a structured mesh of shape <math id="A4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="221\times 51" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>221</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>51</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">221\times 51</annotation></semantics></math>, representing deformations of the NACA-0012 profile, and the output is the Mach number at each mesh point. The dataset includes 1,000 training and 200 test samples with unique airfoil designs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2023b</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A4.SS2.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Pipe.</h4>

<div id="A4.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This benchmark predicts horizontal fluid velocity in pipes with varying internal geometries. Each sample is represented as a <math id="A4.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="129\times 129\times 2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>129</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>129</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">129\times 129\times 2</annotation></semantics></math> tensor encoding mesh point positions, with the output being the velocity at each mesh point (<math id="A4.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="129\times 129\times 1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>129</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>129</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">129\times 129\times 1</annotation></semantics></math>). The dataset consists of 1,000 training and 200 test samples, with pipe shapes generated by controlling the centerline <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2023b</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A4.SS2.SSS0.Px5" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">DrivAerML-40k.</h4>

<div id="A4.SS2.SSS0.Px5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS2.SSS0.Px5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The DrivAerML dataset <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ashton et al., 2024</a>)</cite> has high-fidelity automotive aerodynamic simulations, featuring 500 parametrically morphed DrivAer vehicles.
CFD simulations are performed on 160 million volumetric mesh grids using hybrid RANS-LES, the highest-fidelity scale-resolving CFD approach routinely deployed by the automotive industry <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ashton et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.
Each sample in the dataset includes a surface mesh with approximately 8.8 million points and corresponding pressure values.
Since no official dataset split is provided, an 80/20 random split is used, with 40,000 points sampled per case for training and evaluation.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A4.SS2.SSS0.Px6" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">LPBF.</h4>

<div id="A4.SS2.SSS0.Px6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS2.SSS0.Px6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We introduce the laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) additive manufacturing dataset which involves field prediction on complex geometries.
In metal additive manufacturing, variations in design geometry can affect the dimensional accuracy of the part and lead to shape distortions.
We perform several LPBF process simulations of a set of geometries to obtain the deformation field over the geometry.
We select a subsample of the dataset with up to 50,000 points per geometry and divide it into 1,100 training cases and 290 test cases.
We train models to learn the <math id="A4.SS2.SSS0.Px6.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Z" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>Z</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Z</annotation></semantics></math> (vertical) component of the deformation field at each grid point.
Additional details are provided in <a href="#A8" title="Appendix H Benchmark dataset of additive manufacturing simulations ‣ FLARE: Fast Low-rank Attention Routing Engine" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Appendix H</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
