<div id="A4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We follow the recommended hyperparameter configuration for LNO, Transolver, and GNOT wherever possible.
For consistency, we set the number of blocks to <math id="A4.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B=8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B=8</annotation></semantics></math>,
and strive to match the parameter counts of Transolver without (w/o) convolution for all models.
As such, the hidden feature dimension for vanilla transformer, is set to <math id="A4.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C=80" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>80</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C=80</annotation></semantics></math>.
Its head dimension is set to <math id="A4.SS3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D=16" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>16</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D=16</annotation></semantics></math> and MLP ratio is 4 which is typical for transformers <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Vaswani et al., 2017</a>)</cite>.
For FLARE, we set the hidden feature dimension to <math id="A4.SS3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C=64" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>64</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C=64</annotation></semantics></math>, and use <math id="A4.SS3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H=8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H=8</annotation></semantics></math> or <math id="A4.SS3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="16" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>16</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">16</annotation></semantics></math> heads, which result in a head dimension of <math id="A4.SS3.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D=8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D=8</annotation></semantics></math> or <math id="A4.SS3.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>4</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4</annotation></semantics></math> respectively.
The number of latents is chosen from <math id="A4.SS3.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M\in\{64,\,128,\,256\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>64</mn><mo>,</mo><mn> 128</mn><mo>,</mo><mn> 256</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M\in\{64,\,128,\,256\}</annotation></semantics></math> depending on the problem.
As PerceiverIO was not designed to be a surrogate model,
we generously set its channel dimension to <math id="A4.SS3.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C=128" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>128</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C=128</annotation></semantics></math>, and number of latents to <math id="A4.SS3.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M=1,024" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1,024</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M=1,024</annotation></semantics></math>.
Furthermore, the input and output projections for vanilla transformer, perceiver, and FLARE are held consistent to facilitate an equitable comparison of their point-to-point communication schemes.</p>
</div>
<div id="A4.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate Transolver, GNOT with the hyperparameter configurations provided in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al., 2024</a>)</cite> and LNO on the ones provided in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang and Wang, 2024a</a>)</cite>
on the 2D test cases.
For the remaining problems, we choose the best performing parameter set from the 2D cases.</p>
</div>
<div id="A4.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Unless otherwise stated, all models are trained with the AdamW <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019</a>)</cite> optimizer (<math id="A4.SS3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta_{1}=0.9" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>β</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0.9</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta_{1}=0.9</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A4.SS3.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta_{2}=0.999" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>β</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0.999</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta_{2}=0.999</annotation></semantics></math>) to minimize the relative <math id="A4.SS3.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>L</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> error.
We use the OneCycleLR <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Smith and Topin, 2019</a>)</cite> scheduler with 10% of epochs dedicated to warming-up to a learning rate of <math id="A4.SS3.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10^{-3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10^{-3}</annotation></semantics></math>, followed by cosine decay.
We train on LPBF for 250 epochs, and 500 epochs for all other models.
Note that we use gradient clipping with max_norm<math id="A4.SS3.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="=1.0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mn>1.0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">=1.0</annotation></semantics></math> unless otherwise stated.
Unless otherwise stated, the weight decay regularization parameter is set to <math id="A4.SS3.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10^{-5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10^{-5}</annotation></semantics></math> for the 2D test cases,
<math id="A4.SS3.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10^{-4}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10^{-4}</annotation></semantics></math> for DrivAerML-40k,
and <math id="A4.SS3.p3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10^{-4}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10^{-4}</annotation></semantics></math> for LPBF.
The batch size is set to 2 for the 2D problems and 1 for the 3D problems unless otherwise stated.
Unless otherwise stated, all models are trained in full precision (FP32).</p>
</div>
<section id="A4.SS3.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Vanilla transformer.</h4>

<div id="A4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For the vanilla transformer, we set the hidden feature dimension to <math id="A4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C=80" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>80</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C=80</annotation></semantics></math>, and choose <math id="A4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H=5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H=5</annotation></semantics></math> heads so that the head dimension <math id="A4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D=16" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>16</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D=16</annotation></semantics></math>.
The number of blocks is set to <math id="A4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B=8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B=8</annotation></semantics></math>, and the MLP ratio for the feedforward block is set to 4.
The vanilla transformer can be prohibitively slow for test cases with over 10,000 test points.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A4.SS3.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">PerceiverIO.</h4>

<div id="A4.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For PerceiverIO, we use <math id="A4.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B=8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B=8</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A4.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C=128" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>128</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C=128</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A4.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H=8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H=8</annotation></semantics></math>, and set the latent sequence length to <math id="A4.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M=512" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>512</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M=512</annotation></semantics></math> for all test cases.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A4.SS3.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Transolver.</h4>

<div id="A4.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Transolver (<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al., 2024</a>)</cite>) introduces Physics-Attention: each mesh point is softly assigned to a few learnable <em id="A4.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">slices</em>, shrinking thousands of points to only tens of tokens.
Self-attention runs on this compact set and the tokens are then desliced back to points.
Following the hyperparameter recommendations in the code of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al., 2024</a>)</cite>,
Transolver is trained with 30% of the steps dedicated to warm-up, and gradient clipping with max_norm <math id="A4.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="=0.1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mn>0.1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">=0.1</annotation></semantics></math>.
The recommended batch size for Transolver is 1 for elasticity, and 4 for the remaining 2D problems.
For the 3D problems, we set the batch size to 1.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A4.SS3.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Transolver++.</h4>

<div id="A4.SS3.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS3.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluated Transolver++ using the latest version of the official code release (<a href="https://github.com/thuml/Transolver_plus" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://github.com/thuml/Transolver_plus</a>) together with the hyperparameters reported in the paper.
All experiments were run using PyTorch 2.7 and CUDA 12.8; the supplementary material provides a script to instantiate the standard environment used for all benchmark runs.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A4.SS3.SSS0.Px5" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Latent Neural Operator (LNO).</h4>

<div id="A4.SS3.SSS0.Px5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS3.SSS0.Px5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">LNO (<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang and Wang, 2024b</a>)</cite>) moves computation into a small latent space.
An embedder lifts the input field, cross-attention compresses <math id="A4.SS3.SSS0.Px5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math> points into <math id="A4.SS3.SSS0.Px5.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> latent tokens, transformers act solely on these tokens, and a decoder maps them to any query location.
In line with the recommended hyperparameter configuration in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang and Wang, 2024b</a>)</cite>,
we set <math id="A4.SS3.SSS0.Px5.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta_{2}=0.99" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>β</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0.99</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta_{2}=0.99</annotation></semantics></math> in the AdamW optimizer,
do warmup for the first 20% of epochs,
and clip gradient norms greater than 1,000.
The number of hidden features are set to <math id="A4.SS3.SSS0.Px5.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C=192" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>192</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C=192</annotation></semantics></math> for elasticity, and <math id="A4.SS3.SSS0.Px5.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C=128" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>128</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C=128</annotation></semantics></math> for all other test cases.
The number of residual layers is set to 3 for elasticity and 4 for other test cases.
The number of latent self attention blocks is 8 for pipe and airfoil test cases and 4 for all other cases.
The number of latent modes is set to 256 for all test cases.
The batch size during training is set to 4 for the 2D test cases and 1 for the 3D test cases.
The LNO code also recommends weight decay regularization of <math id="A4.SS3.SSS0.Px5.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="5\cdot 10^{-5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>5</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5\cdot 10^{-5}</annotation></semantics></math> for the 2D test cases.</p>
</div>
<div id="A4.SS3.SSS0.Px5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS3.SSS0.Px5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Through communication with the LNO authors (see <a href="https://github.com/L-I-M-I-T/LatentNeuralOperator/pull/6" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://github.com/L-I-M-I-T/LatentNeuralOperator/pull/6</a>),
we learned that the datasets used in the LNO paper and in the original Transolver paper are not the same.</p>
</div>
<div id="A4.SS3.SSS0.Px5.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS3.SSS0.Px5.p3.1" class="ltx_p">In running our experiments, we noticed discrepancies between our LNO results and those presented in their article <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang and Wang, 2024a</a>)</cite>.
Upon further investigation, we found that the datasets used in the LNO paper and in the original Transolver paper are not the same.
For example, in the Elasticity dataset, LNO was trained and tested on a <math id="A4.SS3.SSS0.Px5.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1000/1000" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1000</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>1000</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1000/1000</annotation></semantics></math> split, whereas Transolver used a <math id="A4.SS3.SSS0.Px5.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1000/200" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1000</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>200</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1000/200</annotation></semantics></math> split.
In the Darcy dataset, LNO employed a higher resolution of <math id="A4.SS3.SSS0.Px5.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="241\times 241" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>241</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>241</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">241\times 241</annotation></semantics></math>, compared to <math id="A4.SS3.SSS0.Px5.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="85\times 85" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>85</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>85</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">85\times 85</annotation></semantics></math> in Transolver.
Because these differences make direct comparison unreliable, all models (including LNO and Transolver) were re-trained and evaluated on the standardized Transolver splits and resolutions to ensure fairness.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A4.SS3.SSS0.Px6" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">General Neural Operator Transformer (GNOT).</h4>

<div id="A4.SS3.SSS0.Px6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS3.SSS0.Px6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">GNOT (<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hao et al., 2023</a>)</cite>) employs heterogeneous normalized attention, separately normalizing keys and values, to fuse multiple input fields on irregular meshes. A learnable geometric gate decomposes the domain and routes tokens to scale-specific expert MLPs. Linear cost attention plus this gating scales to large problems and surpasses earlier operator learners.</p>
</div>
<div id="A4.SS3.SSS0.Px6.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS3.SSS0.Px6.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Following the hyperparameter recommendations outlined in the code of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al., 2024</a>)</cite>,
GNOT is trained with 30% of the steps dedicated to warm-up, and gradient clipping with max_norm = <math id="A4.SS3.SSS0.Px6.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.1</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.1</annotation></semantics></math>.
The recommended batch size for Transolver is 1 for elasticity, and 4 for the remaining 2D problems.
The batch size is set to 2 for elasticity, 4 for the remaining 2D benchmarks and 1 for the 3D benchmarks.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A4.SS3.SSS0.Px7" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">FLARE.</h4>

<div id="A4.SS3.SSS0.Px7.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS3.SSS0.Px7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">All attention operations in FLARE are implemented using <span id="A4.SS3.SSS0.Px7.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">scaled_dot_product_attention</span> (SDPA) in <span id="A4.SS3.SSS0.Px7.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">torch.nn.functional</span>, as shown in <a href="#S3.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 3.2 FLARE: Fast Low-rank Attention Routing Engine ‣ 3 Method ‣ FLARE: Fast Low-rank Attention Routing Engine" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure 3</span></a>; this allows PyTorch to dispatch to fused SDPA backends (e.g., FlashAttention-style kernels) when available.
For all problems, we employ <math id="A4.SS3.SSS0.Px7.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B=8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B=8</annotation></semantics></math> blocks with a feature dimension of <math id="A4.SS3.SSS0.Px7.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C=64" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>64</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C=64</annotation></semantics></math>.
We set the number of residual layers and the number of key/value projection layers to 3, and vary the head dimension as
<math id="A4.SS3.SSS0.Px7.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D\in\{4,8\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D\in\{4,8\}</annotation></semantics></math>,
the number of latent tokens as
<math id="A4.SS3.SSS0.Px7.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M\in\{64,128,256\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>64,128,256</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M\in\{64,128,256\}</annotation></semantics></math>
The hyperparameters for each test case are presented in <a href="#A4.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ D.3 Benchmark models and training details ‣ Appendix D Benchmarking and Comparison ‣ FLARE: Fast Low-rank Attention Routing Engine" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table 5</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A4.F8" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2508.12594v3/time_memory_bwd_fp32.svg" id="A4.F8.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/236;" width="476" height="236"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A4.F8.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 8</span>: </span><span id="A4.F8.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">
Execution times in FP32 for a single vanilla self-attention layer, a physics attention layer, and FLARE.
The models are set to have approximately the same number of parameters as in <a href="#S5.SS1" title="5.1 PDE surrogate benchmarks ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ FLARE: Fast Low-rank Attention Routing Engine" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section 5.1</span></a>.
This calculation is performed on a single H100 80GB GPU.
Note that the curves for FLARE are somewhat overlapping.
</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A5" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix E </span>Field-prediction on million-point geometries</h2>

<section id="A5.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Experimental setup.</h4>

<div id="A5.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We train FLARE on the DrivAerML dataset <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ashton et al., 2024</a>)</cite> using meshes subsampled to contain <math id="A5.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N=10^{6}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mn>6</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N=10^{6}</annotation></semantics></math> points per geometry.
All experiments are run on a single Nvidia H100 80GB GPU with batch size <math id="A5.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1</annotation></semantics></math>.
Unless otherwise stated, models use feature dimension <math id="A5.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C=64" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>64</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C=64</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A5.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H=8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H=8</annotation></semantics></math> attention heads.
We vary the number of latent tokens <math id="A5.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M\in\{128,512,1024,2048\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>128,512</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1024</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2048</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M\in\{128,512,1024,2048\}</annotation></semantics></math> and the number of FLARE blocks <math id="A5.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>B</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B</annotation></semantics></math> (as reported in <a href="#S5.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ Benchmark problems. ‣ 5.1 PDE surrogate benchmarks ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ FLARE: Fast Low-rank Attention Routing Engine" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure 5</span></a>).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A5.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Training details.</h4>

<div id="A5.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">All FLARE models in this study are trained in mixed precision to take advantage of fused SDPA backends (e.g., FlashAttention-style kernels).
We train for 500 epochs with the OneCycleLR scheduler <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Smith and Topin, 2019</a>)</cite> where the first <math id="A5.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="5\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>5</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5\%</annotation></semantics></math> of epochs are spent warming up to a learning rate of <math id="A5.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="5\cdot 10^{-4}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>5</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5\cdot 10^{-4}</annotation></semantics></math> followed by cosine decay.
No hidden sparsity, memory offloading, or distributed training is used.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A6" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix F </span>Discussion on the design principles of FLARE.</h2>

<section id="A6.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Latent tokens enable gather-scatter communication.</h4>

<div id="A6.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In FLARE, information flows through latent tokens by first <span id="A6.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">gathering</span> from the input sequence and then <span id="A6.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">scattering</span> back.
The encoding step can be understood as a gather (all-reduce) operation, where each latent token pools information from the input according to its learned query pattern.
Formally, for latent query <math id="A6.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q_{m}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q_{m}</annotation></semantics></math>,</p>
<table id="A6.E23" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A6.E23.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="z_{m}=\sum_{n=1}^{N}\frac{\exp(q_m \cdot k_n)}{\sum_{n^{\prime}=1}^{N}\exp(q_m \cdot k_{n'})}\,v_{n},\quad m=1,\dots,M," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>z</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>m</mi></msub><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><msup><mrow></mrow><mi>N</mi></msup><mfrac><mrow><mi>exp</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><msubsup><mo>∑</mo><mrow><msup><mi>n</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></msubsup><mrow><mi>exp</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msub><mi>k</mi><msup><mi>n</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mfrac><mi>v</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>n</mi></msub><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>M</mi><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_{m}=\sum_{n=1}^{N}\frac{\exp(q_m \cdot k_n)}{\sum_{n^{\prime}=1}^{N}\exp(q_m \cdot k_{n'})}\,v_{n},\quad m=1,\dots,M,</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(23)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A6.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.2" class="ltx_p"><math id="A6.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z_{m}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_{m}</annotation></semantics></math> aggregates input values <math id="A6.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v_{n}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v_{n}</annotation></semantics></math> with convex weights.
When the similarity scores are sharp, <math id="A6.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z_{m}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_{m}</annotation></semantics></math> emphasizes a few dominant inputs; when they are flatter, <math id="A6.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z_{m}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_{m}</annotation></semantics></math> acts like a specialized <span id="A6.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">pooling token</span> that averages a select set of tokens.
Across <math id="A6.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> latents, this yields a compact set of global descriptors, each specializing in pooling different aspects of the input.</p>
</div>
<div id="A6.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The decoding step is the dual scatter (broadcast) operation, but importantly, the broadcast is <span id="A6.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">selective</span>: each latent <math id="A6.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z_{m}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_{m}</annotation></semantics></math> contributes only to the input tokens that assigned it high weight in the encoding step.
Concretely,</p>
<table id="A6.E24" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A6.E24.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="y_{n}=\sum_{m=1}^{M}\frac{\exp(k_n \cdot q_m)}{\sum_{m^{\prime}=1}^{M}\exp(k_n \cdot q_{m'})}\,z_{m},\quad n=1,\dots,N," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>n</mi></msub><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><msup><mrow></mrow><mi>M</mi></msup><mfrac><mrow><mi>exp</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>m</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><msubsup><mo>∑</mo><mrow><msup><mi>m</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>M</mi></msubsup><mrow><mi>exp</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msub><mi>q</mi><msup><mi>m</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mfrac><mi>z</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>m</mi></msub><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y_{n}=\sum_{m=1}^{M}\frac{\exp(k_n \cdot q_m)}{\sum_{m^{\prime}=1}^{M}\exp(k_n \cdot q_{m'})}\,z_{m},\quad n=1,\dots,N,</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(24)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A6.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.2" class="ltx_p">the output token <math id="A6.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y_{n}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y_{n}</annotation></semantics></math> only receives substantial information from the latents whose query pattern matches its key <math id="A6.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k_{n}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k_{n}</annotation></semantics></math> strongly.
In this sense, each latent acts as both a selective <span id="A6.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">pooling hub</span> and <span id="A6.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">broadcaster</span>, routing information back along the pathways that originally recruited it.
Together, these gather-scatter stages form a low-rank, butterfly-like transformation: first contracting <math id="A6.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math> tokens into <math id="A6.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M\ll N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>≪</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M\ll N</annotation></semantics></math> global features, and then expanding back to <math id="A6.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math> outputs, enabling efficient, yet expressive, global communication.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A6.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Symmetry in latent token communication.</h4>

<div id="A6.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The compression–expansion attention structure in FLARE is most effective when the encoding and decoding operators are structurally aligned.
Specifically, <math id="A6.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{\text{encode},h}=\mathrm{softmax}(Q_{h}\cdot K_{h}^{T})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mrow><mtext>encode</mtext><mo>,</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>softmax</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>Q</mi><mi>h</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msubsup><mi>K</mi><mi>h</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{\text{encode},h}=\mathrm{softmax}(Q_{h}\cdot K_{h}^{T})</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A6.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{\text{decode},h}=\mathrm{softmax}(K_{h}\cdot Q_{h}^{T})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mrow><mtext>decode</mtext><mo>,</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>softmax</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>K</mi><mi>h</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msubsup><mi>Q</mi><mi>h</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{\text{decode},h}=\mathrm{softmax}(K_{h}\cdot Q_{h}^{T})</annotation></semantics></math> are transposes of each other up to diagonal scaling.
We experimented with breaking this symmetry by using distinct query–key pairs for encoding and decoding, but observed no accuracy gains.
This suggests that the near-adjoint relationship between <math id="A6.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{\text{encode}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>W</mi><mtext>encode</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{\text{encode}}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A6.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{\text{decode}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>W</mi><mtext>decode</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{\text{decode}}</annotation></semantics></math>, both derived from the same parameters, may provide a form of mathematical optimality, ensuring stable information flow through latent tokens while reducing representational redundancy.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A6.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Tradeoff between query dynamics and key/value expressivity.</h4>

<div id="A6.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">An important design choice in FLARE is to use fixed, input-independent queries <math id="A6.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Q" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>Q</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q</annotation></semantics></math>, which constrain the flexibility of the attention pattern.
Detaching <math id="A6.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Q" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>Q</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q</annotation></semantics></math> from <math id="A6.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>X</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X</annotation></semantics></math> allows for the low-rank communication structure, but requires compensating expressivity in the key and value projections.
In practice, we find that deeper residual MLPs for <math id="A6.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A6.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>V</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V</annotation></semantics></math> are crucial for capturing rich, feature interactions under this constraint.
Conversely, one could imagine making <math id="A6.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Q" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>Q</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q</annotation></semantics></math> dynamic by conditioning it on <math id="A6.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>X</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X</annotation></semantics></math>, which would shift more of the modeling burden to the query side and potentially allow shallower <math id="A6.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K,V" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>V</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K,V</annotation></semantics></math> projections.
Thus, FLARE embodies a clear tradeoff: fixing <math id="A6.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Q" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>Q</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q</annotation></semantics></math> encourages stability and efficiency, but places greater importance on the depth and expressivity of the key/value encoders.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A7" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix G </span>Model analysis and ablations</h2>

<figure id="A7.F9" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2508.12594v3/abl_num_blocks_elasticity.svg" id="A7.F9.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:235/156;" width="235" height="156"></object></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2508.12594v3/abl_num_blocks_darcy.svg" id="A7.F9.g2" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:235/156;" width="235" height="156"></object></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A7.F9.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 9</span>: </span><span id="A7.F9.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">
Effect of number of blocks (<math id="A7.F9.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>B</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B</annotation></semantics></math>) and number of latent tokens (<math id="A7.F9.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math>) on test accuracy on the Elasticity (left) and Darcy (right) test cases. Experiment details are presented in <a href="#A7" title="Appendix G Model analysis and ablations ‣ FLARE: Fast Low-rank Attention Routing Engine" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Appendix G</span></a>.
</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Time and memory complexity.</h4>

<div id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><a href="#S1.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ FLARE: Fast Low-rank Attention Routing Engine" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure 2</span></a> illustrates the time and memory complexity of a single forward and backward pass for different attention schemes on long sequences.
The experiment is done in mixed precision (FP16 in forward pass, FP32 in backward pass) using PyTorch’s autocast functionality with <math id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C=128" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>128</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C=128</annotation></semantics></math> features and <math id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H=8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H=8</annotation></semantics></math> heads for all models.
The FlashAttention backend <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dao et al., 2022</a>)</cite> is employed for SDPA wherever possible.</p>
</div>
<div id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Although vanilla self-attention has the lowest memory cost thanks to the FlashAttention algorithm, which eliminates the need to materialize the score matrices (<math id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Q_{h}\cdot K_{h}^{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>Q</mi><mi>h</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msubsup><mi>K</mi><mi>h</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q_{h}\cdot K_{h}^{T}</annotation></semantics></math>), its compute time still scales poorly with the sequence length.
In contrast, the compute time for FLARE exhibits strong scaling with sequence length.
Its memory requirement is marginally greater than vanilla attention due to the presence of deep residual networks for key/value projections, and due to the need to materialize <math id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Z_{h}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>Z</mi><mi>h</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Z_{h}</annotation></semantics></math>, the latent sequence of <math id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> tokens.
As these costs are marginal compared to the SDPA operation, the curves for different <math id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> values of FLARE are somewhat overlapping.
Finally, the compute time for Physics Attention of Transolver <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al., 2024</a>)</cite> exhibits somewhat good scaling.
However, its memory cost and compute time blow up for large slice counts due to the need for materializing the projection matrices.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Number of blocks (<math id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>B</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B</annotation></semantics></math>) and latent tokens (<math id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math>).</h4>

<div id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><a href="#A7.F9" title="Figure 9 ‣ Appendix G Model analysis and ablations ‣ FLARE: Fast Low-rank Attention Routing Engine" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure 9</span></a> presents the test relative error of FLARE on the Elasticity (left) and Darcy (right) benchmark datasets as a function of the number of blocks <math id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(B)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(B)</annotation></semantics></math> and the number of latent tokens <math id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(M)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>M</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(M)</annotation></semantics></math>.
<a href="#S5.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ Benchmark problems. ‣ 5.1 PDE surrogate benchmarks ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ FLARE: Fast Low-rank Attention Routing Engine" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure 5</span></a> (left) presents the same for the DrivAerML dataset with one million points per geometry.
In all cases, we note the favorable trend that relative error consistently decreases as we increase the number of blocks.
Similarly, we observe that the relative error generally decreases with <math id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math>, though the trend is not strictly monotonic.
In the Elasticity problem, improvements with rank diminish rapidly, indicating that global communication in that problem is fundamentally low-rank.
On the other hand, increasing <math id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> monotonically increases performance on the Darcy problem, indicating that the problem is <em id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">rank-limited</em>.
This also explains why vanilla transformer with a full-rank attention pattern outperforms rank-deficient FLARE on the darcy problem.
However, the accuracy gain comes at the cost of greater latency as the vanilla transformer is <math id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m5" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\sim 5\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>∼</mo><mn>5</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim 5\times</annotation></semantics></math> slower than FLARE on the Darcy problem.
<a href="#S5.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ Benchmark problems. ‣ 5.1 PDE surrogate benchmarks ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ FLARE: Fast Low-rank Attention Routing Engine" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure 5</span></a> indicates that time per epoch (middle) and memory (right) scaling of FLARE with <math id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>B</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math>.
Here, increasing <math id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> leads to increased latency, and that increasing <math id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> does not come at the cost of greater memory requirements.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A7.F10" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2508.12594v3/abl_num_layers_elasticity.svg" id="A7.F10.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/149;" width="476" height="149"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A7.F10.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 10</span>: </span><span id="A7.F10.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">
(Left) effect of the number of residual layers in key/ value projection, and (right) of residual layers in residual block on test accuracy.
In both cases, deeper networks lead to greater accuracy.
</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="A7.F11" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2508.12594v3/abl_lb.png" id="A7.F11.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:333/270;" width="333" height="270" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A7.F11.6" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 11</span>: </span><span id="A7.F11.7" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">
<span id="A7.F11.7.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Ablation on the number of latent-space self-attention blocks (<math id="A7.F11.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L_{B}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>B</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L_{B}</annotation></semantics></math>) versus the number of FLARE encode-decode blocks (<math id="A7.F11.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>B</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B</annotation></semantics></math>).</span>
Each cell reports: (top) test relative error, (middle) parameter count, and (bottom) training time per epoch.
The total cost of a model with <math id="A7.F11.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>B</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B</annotation></semantics></math> FLARE blocks and <math id="A7.F11.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L_{B}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>B</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L_{B}</annotation></semantics></math> latent blocks is
<math id="A7.F11.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{O}(B\,NM+BL_{B}\,M^{2})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>N</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>B</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>M</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}(B\,NM+BL_{B}\,M^{2})</annotation></semantics></math>.
The results show that increasing the number of latent-space blocks, as done in LNO-style and Perceiver-style models, yields worse accuracy and poorer speed/parameter tradeoffs than allocating compute to additional FLARE blocks.
The optimal regime lies near the <em id="A7.F11.7.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">top-right corner</em>: many encode-decode blocks and <em id="A7.F11.7.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">zero</em> latent-space blocks.
</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="A7.F12" class="ltx_figure">

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A7.F12.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 12</span>: </span><span id="A7.F12.6" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">

Each plot shows the <math id="A7.F12.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M{=}64" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>64</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M{=}64</annotation></semantics></math> nonzero eigenvalues of the head-specific communication matrices <math id="A7.F12.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{h}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>h</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{h}</annotation></semantics></math> (<a href="#S3.E9" title="Equation 9 ‣ Low-rank communication. ‣ 3.2 FLARE: Fast Low-rank Attention Routing Engine ‣ 3 Method ‣ FLARE: Fast Low-rank Attention Routing Engine" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Eq. 9</span></a>) for FLARE with <math id="A7.F12.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B{=}8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B{=}8</annotation></semantics></math> blocks and <math id="A7.F12.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C{=}64" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>64</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C{=}64</annotation></semantics></math> features trained on the elasticity dataset.
When heads share a single latent sequence (top row), the eigenvalue spectra across heads are nearly identical, indicating similar learned low-rank subspaces.
When heads use independent latent slices (bottom row), the eigenvalue decay varies noticeably across heads, reflecting more diverse low-rank structures.
The accompanying table reports test relative errors for different depths <math id="A7.F12.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>B</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B</annotation></semantics></math>, showing that models with independent latents consistently achieve lower error.
</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">ResMLP depth: key/value projections.</h4>

<div id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A substantial distinction between vanilla self-attention and FLARE is the introduction of deep residual blocks for key and value projections in place of simple linear layers.
In standard self-attention, queries (<math id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Q_{h}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>Q</mi><mi>h</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q_{h}</annotation></semantics></math>) and keys (<math id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K_{h}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>K</mi><mi>h</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K_{h}</annotation></semantics></math>) determine the global communication pattern through <math id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{h}=\mathrm{softmax}(Q_{h}K_{h}^{T}/s)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>h</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>softmax</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>Q</mi><mi>h</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>K</mi><mi>h</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup></mrow><mo>/</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{h}=\mathrm{softmax}(Q_{h}K_{h}^{T}/s)</annotation></semantics></math>, while values (<math id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V_{h}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>h</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V_{h}</annotation></semantics></math>) carry the information to be communicated.
All three are typically computed as shallow linear projections of the input <math id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>X</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X</annotation></semantics></math>.
In contrast, FLARE computes the attention pattern as <math id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{h}=\mathrm{softmax}(K_{h}Q_{h}^{T})\cdot\mathrm{softmax}(Q_{h}K_{h}^{T})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>h</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>softmax</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>K</mi><mi>h</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>Q</mi><mi>h</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup></mrow><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mrow><mi>softmax</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>Q</mi><mi>h</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>K</mi><mi>h</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{h}=\mathrm{softmax}(K_{h}Q_{h}^{T})\cdot\mathrm{softmax}(Q_{h}K_{h}^{T})</annotation></semantics></math>, where the query embeddings <math id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Q_{h}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>Q</mi><mi>h</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q_{h}</annotation></semantics></math> are learned parameters independent of the input.
This makes the attention pattern less dynamic, motivating architectural modifications to enhance flexibility.</p>
</div>
<div id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To address this, we replace the linear key and value projections with deep residual MLPs.
Using residual networks for key and value encodings allows each token to learn richer and more structured features rather than shallow embeddings, which is particularly crucial in FLARE since the queries are fixed and cannot adapt to the input.
<a href="#A7.F10" title="Figure 10 ‣ Number of blocks (𝐵) and latent tokens (𝑀). ‣ Appendix G Model analysis and ablations ‣ FLARE: Fast Low-rank Attention Routing Engine" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure 10</span></a> (left) shows the impact of varying the number of residual layers in key/value projections and within the residual block on test accuracy for the elasticity benchmark dataset.
We suspect that deeper key/value encodings lead to more meaningful and focused attention, encoding structured inductive priors beneficial to downstream prediction.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">ResMLP depth: feedforward block.</h4>

<div id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A second difference between the standard attention block and FLARE block is that we replace the feed-forward block in vanilla self-attention with a deep residual MLP.
Preliminary experiments using standard feed-forward blocks led to training instabilities and poor convergence.
In contrast, residual MLPs consistently enabled stable training and allowed us to increase model capacity.
<a href="#A7.F10" title="Figure 10 ‣ Number of blocks (𝐵) and latent tokens (𝑀). ‣ Appendix G Model analysis and ablations ‣ FLARE: Fast Low-rank Attention Routing Engine" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure 10</span></a> (right) indicates that increasing the number of residual layers leads to slight improvements in accuracy.
Based on these results, we use three residual layers in both key/value projections and the residual block, as this provides a good trade-off between model capacity and computational cost in all subsequent experiments.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A7.F13" class="ltx_figure" style="width:50%;"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2508.12594v3/abl_num_heads_elasticity.svg" id="A7.F13.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:238/199;" width="238" height="199"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A7.F13.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 13</span>: </span><span id="A7.F13.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">
Effect of head dimension (<math id="A7.F13.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>D</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D</annotation></semantics></math>) on test accuracy.
We design FLARE to work optimally for <math id="A7.F13.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D=4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D=4</annotation></semantics></math>–<math id="A7.F13.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>8</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">8</annotation></semantics></math>.
</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px5" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Effect of head dimension and parallel low-rank projections.</h4>

<div id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A core hypothesis underlying FLARE is that each attention head implements an independent rank–<math id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\leq M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≤</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\leq M</annotation></semantics></math> projection–reconstruction pathway.
When multiple such pathways operate in parallel, the resulting attention operator becomes a mixture of low-rank factors, each capturing a distinct structural component of the underlying communication pattern.
This is in contrast to Transolver, which shares projection weights across all heads, and LNO, which uses a single global projection: both designs restrict the model to learning at most one or a few shared low-rank directions.
FLARE, by contrast, allows each head to specialize in complementary routing patterns by
assigning it an independent slice of the latent tokens.</p>
</div>
<div id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To examine this hypothesis quantitatively, we vary the number of heads <math id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>H</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H</annotation></semantics></math> while keeping the total feature dimension <math id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C=64" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>64</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C=64</annotation></semantics></math> and number of blocks <math id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B=8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B=8</annotation></semantics></math> fixed, thereby trading off head dimension <math id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D=C/H" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>H</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D=C/H</annotation></semantics></math> against the number of parallel low-rank projections available to the model.
As shown in <a href="#A7.F13" title="Figure 13 ‣ ResMLP depth: feedforward block. ‣ Appendix G Model analysis and ablations ‣ FLARE: Fast Low-rank Attention Routing Engine" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure 13</span></a>, FLARE consistently achieves the best accuracy for <math id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D=4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D=4</annotation></semantics></math> or <math id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D=8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D=8</annotation></semantics></math>, outperforming configurations with larger head dimensions.
This behavior is the reverse of what is commonly observed in standard transformers—where typical head
dimensions are <math id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D=16" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>16</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D=16</annotation></semantics></math>–<math id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="32" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>32</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">32</annotation></semantics></math>, but is entirely consistent with FLARE’s architectural role for each head.
Larger <math id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>D</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D</annotation></semantics></math> increases the per-head representational capacity but reduces the number of parallel low-rank factors; smaller <math id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>D</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D</annotation></semantics></math> yields more distinct heads, and thereby more distinct projection–reconstruction pathways, which better approximate a full attention map.</p>
</div>
<div id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We additionally note a practical implication of this analysis: because the dot-product magnitudes are naturally small for <math id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D\in\{4,8\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D\in\{4,8\}</annotation></semantics></math>, we use a scaling factor of <math id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1</annotation></semantics></math> rather than the usual <math id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1/\sqrt{D}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><msqrt><mi>D</mi></msqrt></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1/\sqrt{D}</annotation></semantics></math> in these cases, simplifying implementation without sacrificing stability.
Overall, the head-dimension ablation strongly supports our main architectural claim: FLARE benefits from <em id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p3.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">multiple parallel low-rank projections</em>, and enabling per-head independence is crucial for capturing diverse communication patterns.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px6" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Ablation on latent-space blocks vs. FLARE blocks.</h4>

<div id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To directly investigate whether FLARE’s encode-decode mechanism is responsible for the observed performance gains, we conduct a controlled ablation varying the number of latent-space self-attention blocks (<math id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L_{B}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>B</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L_{B}</annotation></semantics></math>) and the number of full FLARE blocks (<math id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>B</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B</annotation></semantics></math>).
This experiment spans the continuum between a Perceiver/LNO-like architecture (few encode-decode operations and many latent-space blocks; bottom-left of <a href="#A7.F11" title="Figure 11 ‣ Number of blocks (𝐵) and latent tokens (𝑀). ‣ Appendix G Model analysis and ablations ‣ FLARE: Fast Low-rank Attention Routing Engine" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure 11</span></a>) and a FLARE-like architecture (many encode-decode blocks and no latent-space self-attention; top-right).</p>
</div>
<div id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Across all parameter budgets, we observe a consistent trend: <em id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">increasing the number of latent-space blocks degrades accuracy while increasing computational cost</em>.
Latent-space self-attention contributes additional parameters and a <math id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{O}(M^{2})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>M</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}(M^{2})</annotation></semantics></math> cost per block, yet does not improve the model’s ability to capture global structure.
In contrast, allocating the same compute to additional encode-decode blocks, which perform low-rank global mixing via cross-attention, steadily improves accuracy.
The lowest errors in the entire grid occur in the top-right corner, corresponding to <em id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p2.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">zero</em> latent-space blocks and the largest number of FLARE blocks.</p>
</div>
<div id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p3.1" class="ltx_p">This ablation provides direct causal evidence supporting FLARE’s architectural choice: global communication is most effectively learned by repeating the low-rank projection/unprojection pathway, not by performing nonlinear refinements inside the latent space.
If one interprets the Perceiver <math id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\leftrightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">↔</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\leftrightarrow</annotation></semantics></math> FLARE spectrum as trading latent refinement for repeated global mixing, our results show that the optimal regime is decisively FLARE-like.
For a fixed parameter budget and wall-clock time, the best strategy is to <em id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p3.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">reduce or eliminate latent-space attention and increase the number of encode-decode blocks</em>, validating the design principle that token mixing should occur through repeated low-rank attention projections rather than deeper latent-space transformers.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px7" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Ablation on shared vs. independent per-head latent tokens.</h4>

<div id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px7.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To assess the effect of head-wise latent diversity—central to FLARE’s design, we compare two variants: (i) <em id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px7.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">shared-latent</em> models, where all heads use the same latent sequence, and (ii) <em id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px7.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">independent-latent</em> models, where each head receives its own slice of the latent tokens.
This isolates whether FLARE’s expressivity arises merely from the low-rank encode-decode structure or whether the ability of different heads to learn distinct low-rank projections provides additional modeling capacity.</p>
</div>
<div id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px7.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px7.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The spectral plots in <a href="#A7.F12" title="Figure 12 ‣ Number of blocks (𝐵) and latent tokens (𝑀). ‣ Appendix G Model analysis and ablations ‣ FLARE: Fast Low-rank Attention Routing Engine" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure 12</span></a> reveal a clear difference between the two settings.
With shared latents, all heads exhibit nearly identical eigenvalue decay, implying that they compress and propagate information in similar ways.
In contrast, independent latents produce noticeably different spectra across heads, particularly in deeper blocks, indicating that different heads discover complementary low-rank subspaces of the token-to-token communication structure.
This diversity is modest in early layers but becomes increasingly pronounced as depth increases.</p>
</div>
<div id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px7.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A7.SS0.SSS0.Px7.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Crucially, the quantitative results mirror this qualitative behavior: across all depths, models with independent per-head latents achieve lower test relative error despite having comparable parameter counts.
This provides causal evidence—not just descriptive visualization—that head-wise independence is beneficial.
It supports our claim that FLARE’s mixture of head-specific low-rank projections yields richer communication pathways than architectures that use a single shared projection (e.g., Transolver) or a single latent transformer (e.g., LNO, PerceiverIO).
Finally, we note that applying the same spectral analysis to Transolver or LNO is not directly meaningful, since their latent-space transformations are nonlinear and not expressible as a single linear low-rank operator; FLARE’s structure uniquely enables such eigenanalysis.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A8" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix H </span>Benchmark dataset of additive manufacturing simulations</h2>

<figure id="A8.F14" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2508.12594v3/lpbf_gallery.png" id="A8.F14.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:381/267;" width="381" height="267" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A8.F14.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 14</span>: </span><span id="A8.F14.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">
We simulate the LPBF process on selected geometries from the Autodesk segmentation dataset <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lambourne et al., 2021</a>)</cite> to generate a benchmark dataset for AM calculations.
Several geometries are presented in this gallery.
The color indicates <math id="A8.F14.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Z" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>Z</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Z</annotation></semantics></math> (vertical) displacement field.
</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="A8.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">H.1 </span>Introduction &amp; Background</h3>

<div id="A8.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A8.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In metal additive manufacturing (AM), subtle variations in design geometry and process parameter selection may result in undesirable part artifacts or even costly build failures.
Numerical simulations of laser powder bed fusion (LPBF), a popular additive manufacturing process, can be used to predict build failures, but this may take several minutes to hours depending on the part size.</p>
</div>
<div id="A8.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A8.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Although AM enables the fabrication of a wide variety of new designs, the final product must nonetheless comply with the constraints of the underlying manufacturing process.
Metal AM parts often have anisotropic and spatially varying material properties that depend on geometric features (such as overhang, or support structure) and fabrication process parameters (such as laser energy density, hatch spacing, layer thickness, and raster path).
As-built parts with thin features often suffer distortions when manufactured with the LPBF process, which uses a high-power laser to selectively melt and fuse metal powder, layer-by-layer, to create complex, high-precision parts.
Thermal stresses, termed <em id="A8.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">residual stresses</em> (RS), accumulate in LPBF-fabricated parts as a result of rapid thermal cycling due to laser exposure.
These stresses can be severe to the point of inducing localized plastic deformations or delamination.
As such, due to these <em id="A8.SS1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">residual deformations</em>, the final shape of the part may deviate from the designed geometry.</p>
</div>
<div id="A8.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A8.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We present a high-fidelity thermomechanical RS calculation data set on the Fusion 360 segmentation dataset, a publicly available dataset of complex 3D geometries <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lambourne et al., 2021</a>)</cite>.
Numerical solvers for simulating the LPBF build process perform expensive quasi-static thermo-mechanical equations,</p>
<table id="A8.E25" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">
